steps.text: Part 2 of 4: Piece values: counting what you win and lose. This part covers Add and subtract. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

Most captures are not free, because the other side can capture back. To judge a capture, **add what you take and subtract what you lose**. The result is the points you gain or lose in the swap. A swap that leaves you ahead is usually a good one when nothing else is going on, even if you lose a piece. Watch three swaps next.

steps.caption: A bishop can take a rook, but a pawn guards it. Add and subtract.

line.say: The bishop takes the rook: 5 points in.
The pawn takes the bishop back: 3 points out. Five minus three is plus two.

claims.statement: White comes out at least 2 points ahead.

steps.caption: Now the other way round. A queen can take a pawn, but a pawn guards it.

line.say: The queen takes the pawn: only 1 point in.
The pawn takes the queen: 9 points out. One minus nine is minus eight.

claims.statement: White ends the swap 8 points down.
The capture is a serious mistake.

steps.caption: A rook can take a rook, and a pawn guards it. Equal pieces cancel out.

line.say: The rook takes the rook: 5 points in.
The pawn takes the rook back: 5 points out. Five minus five is zero: an even swap.

steps.caption: A small piece can take a big one. A pawn can take a knight, even though the queen takes the pawn back.

line.say: The pawn takes the knight: 3 points in.
The queen takes the pawn: 1 point out. Three minus one is plus two.

steps.caption: Longer swaps work the same way: keep a running total. A pawn is guarded by a rook, and White has two rooks lined up.

line.say: The first rook takes the pawn: running total plus 1.
The black rook takes it: minus 5, so minus 4.
The second rook takes the rook: plus 5, so plus 1. Black has nothing left to take with.

claims.statement: One white rook attacks the pawn directly; the other stands behind it.

steps.caption: Count attackers and defenders. White attacks d5 three times and Black guards it twice. The knight goes first: it is the cheapest attacker.

line.say: The knight takes the pawn: 1 in.
The pawn takes the knight: 3 out, running total minus 2.
A rook takes the pawn: 1 in, minus 1.
The black rook takes it: 5 out, minus 6.
The last rook takes the rook: 5 in. White ends one point down.

claims.statement: Two white pieces attack d5 directly; the second rook backs up the first.
The whole sequence ends one point down.

steps.text: **Count, then decide.** List the attackers and defenders of the square, cheapest first. Either side may stop at any moment, so before each capture ask whether it improves your running total; if not, leave the rest. Three attackers against two defenders sounds like a win, yet the board above ends a point down.

steps.title: Same trade, one change
steps.prompt: A rook defended by a pawn is captured. Predict first what the capture does to White's points. Then see what changes when the capturing piece changes, and when only the colours change.
